pending_items.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
pending_items.content:
In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report , which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face .

In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.

Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.

And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.

"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.

Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban .

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.

Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.

"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls . Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities . Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.

According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.

Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.

"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.

The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.

"This is not just about individual acts of persecution , but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."

Mutasem argues that a failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.

According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.

Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."

Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.

This article was originally written in German

pending_items.title: In Lebanon, the opening of a second airport reflects political shifts
pending_items.content:
KLEIAT AIRPORT, Lebanon, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Lebanon plans to open a second international airport next month to bring economic growth to the poorer north, in a project that underlines the diminished political sway of the Hezbollah group, which had long opposed it.

Kleiat Airport, located on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 km (12 miles) from the border crossing to Syria, will offer another gateway to Lebanon alongside Beirut international airport, where travel has been disrupted by wars between Israel and Hezbollah in recent years.

The opening comes as Lebanon continues to grapple with occupation by Israel in the south, political dysfunction and deep financial turmoil. It is "a national economic need", Fayez Rasamny, the minister of public works and transport, told Reuters. The private sector will invest $5 million to $6 million in the airport and the government will improve the region's roads, Rasamny added.

Also named ReneMouawad Airport after a president assassinated in 1989, it will initially offer flights to Turkey, Egypt, and Jordan, Rasamnysaid.

Politicians from the north had long pressed for the disused airbaseatKleiat to be turned into a civilian airport, arguing it would boost prosperity in the Akkar region, a predominantly Sunni Muslim area adjoining the Syrian border. More than 300,000 people live in Akkar and the region is seen as Lebanon's poorest.

But the idea faced opposition from Hezbollah, an armed Shi'ite Muslim group backed by Iran that long had a decisive say over government affairs, a politician and a political activist from the area told Reuters.

Hadi Hobeich, a former lawmaker from Akkar, said he and a group of MPs from the region had tried to advance the project in 2022, winning the approval of all parties apart from Hezbollah.

Hobeich, a long-standing critic of Hezbollah, said the group had raised concerns over who would be responsible for security at the airport and had shown "intense hostility" towards the idea at the time.

"When the country's political conditions changed, we were able to open this airport," he said.

Hezbollah's media office didn't respond to a request for comment.

Lebanon's power balance has been turned on its head since 2024, when Israel pummelled Hezbollah in two wars in under two years and Syria's president, Bashar al-Assad, a Hezbollah ally, was ousted, severely weakening the group's grip over Lebanese government affairs.

Assad had also opposed the airport, fearing it might fall under the purview of a hostile security force, a senior politician close to Hezbollah said.

Since taking office in early 2025, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has pursued a government policy aimed at securing Hezbollah's disarmament.

His agenda also included opening Kleiat airport.

The government has awarded a four-year concession to a private sector company, Sky Lounge, to run the airport under a public-private partnership.

Sky Lounge Chairman Ziad Monla said the government wants the airport open "as fast as possible". "The north has been forgotten for 30 or 40 years," he told Reuters.

He envisages a hub serving both Syrian and Lebanese passengers and hopes the government can earn up to $20 million from it over four years.

Sky Lounge said it hasso far signed with a local airline to run flights from the new airport, while negotiations with regional and international carriers remain ongoing.

When Reuters visited the airport in early November, dozens of workers buzzed around a hangar being transformed into a passenger terminal. Inside, cables snaked across the floor and scaffolding stood against bare walls.

Hamed Zakariasaid hehas been lobbying officials to open Kleiat Airport for more than a decade. A local political activist and businessman, he hopes the new airport will be a boon for what he sees as a neglected region.

"Akkar is for development, for prosperity," he said.

(Editing by Tom Perry and Alexandra Hudson)

pending_items.title: ‘Second home’: Why Israel is celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
pending_items.content:
When Jensen Huang returned to lead the chip giant Nvidia this week after a scandal over his extramarital affairs, US President Donald Trump was not the only head of government to welcome his second coming.

Thousands of kilometres away, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was celebrating too.

Huang once called Israel Nvidia’s “second home”, and Netanyahu reflected that feeling as he wrote on X: “Nvidia’s partnership with Israel’s tech sector has created enormous value for the company and for Israel’s innovation economy.”

“Continuity in Nvidia’s leadership is good news for that partnership and for the global AI industry,” Netanyahu added, referring to Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president on Monday.

Global headlines have focused on Huang’s affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset; his resignation’s implications for the AI industry; and the larger technology race between Washington and Beijing. His reinstatement at the company he cofounded has gone a long way to settle market jitters. Nvidia’s share price rocketed up by 30 percent on Monday.

But Huang’s return has also calmed nerves in Israel – arguably the country most impacted by Nvidia’s performance outside the United States as it hosts the US-based company’s largest overseas operations.

California-based Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company with a market capitalisation of about $4 trillion, holds the key to the modern artificial intelligence revolution. Huang’s company holds an extraordinary near-90 percent share of the global market for GPUs – graphics processing units, which are specialised AI processors used in AI data centres.

Nvidia’s operations in Israel are its largest in research and development outside the US. It has doubled employees there in the past three years to 6,000 people across seven research and development centres in Yokne’am, Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Ra’anana and Beersheba. It also has plans to build a major research and development campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa to accommodate up to 10,000 employees.

The Bank of Israel has estimated that Nvidia’s work in the country alone will add 2.2 percentage points of growth to Israel’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, bringing it to 5.6 percent. Without Nvidia, that would be 3.4 percent growth, or 40 percent lower.

Next year, Nvidia is expected to add a further 2.4 percentage points to its GDP growth.

Nvidia paid about $1.29bn in taxes to Israel in its financial year that ended in January, according to its annual report. The company is projected to account for nearly 3 percent of Israel’s total state tax revenues in 2026, according to some estimates.

Huang’s resignation on November 12 initially rattled investors on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) with the benchmark indices sliding after the announcement.

But by the end of the day, they had recovered. The TA-35 index finished 0.22 per cent higher at the close of the day while the broader TA-125 gained 0.07 per cent. The BlueTech Global Index, which tracks technology companies, fell 0.15 per cent.

The Haaretz newspaper reported, however, that officials at Israel’s Ministry of Finance were concerned about the potential consequences for the Israeli economy of turmoil – and particularly Huang’s exit – at Nvidia.

On Monday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog congratulated Huang on his return, noting “his deep appreciation to Huang for his continued support for Israel and for his commitment to strengthening the connection between Nvidia and Israel”.

Herzog’s office said Huang told the president that he was “moved by the message and that he intends to make the most of the second chance he has been given”.

Nvidia is helping fuel Israel’s economic machine during its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.

But Israel is also returning strong numbers for the company.

The root of the tech giant’s relationship with the country can be traced back to Nvidia’s acquisition of Mellanox, an Israeli company that supplies computer networking products, in April 2020 for nearly $7bn. That acquisition was central to Nvidia’s success.

Nvidia was already able to make powerful engines that process AI workloads, but a single GPU cannot handle that workload and needs to exchange information with other GPUs.

Mellanox made the networking infrastructure that allows those engines to work together at a fast pace, creating the foundational structure of a data centre.

Nvidia’s networking business, built around Mellanox, generated more than $21bn in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That’s about 18 percent of Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue.

At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January, Huang spoke about Israel’s role in the development of key Nvidia chips.

“Nvidia’s BlueField-4 DPU and three networking components – the ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, NVLink 6 Switch and Spectrum-6 Ethernet Switch – all came out of Israel. So four out of six chips came out of Israel,” he said, praising the employees in Israel.

“Pretty amazing and maybe next time, six out of six chips,” Huang added.

A review by the American Friends Service Committee, a group that won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947 partly for its work rescuing and providing relief to Jews during the Holocaust, has found that the Israeli military uses multiple Nvidia products.

Several purchases of Nvidia products were disclosed by the Israeli Ministry of Defence during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, a report by the group last year noted.

“They include products that are designed for AI applications, like Jetson cards and DGX,” it said, adding that since the public database only records unclassified contracts, “this likely represents only part of the full scale of the military’s usage of Nvidia products and services.”

Israel has made extensive use of AI systems in the Gaza war – including those known as The Gospel, Lavender and Where’s Daddy? – to track and target Palestinians at an unprecedented scale, the group said, adding that Nvidia “could therefore be potentially implicated in these war crimes”.

The Nvidia Jetson TX2 AI processor is also reportedly integrated into Elbit Systems’ Lanius drones, which Israel has used to kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

pending_items.title: Trump to meet Abdul El-Sayed: Will he agree to a renamed Medicare-for-all?
pending_items.content:
United States President Donald Trump says he will meet Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat’s push for a single, low-cost government health insurance programme, which El-Sayed has suggested renaming “Trumpcare”.

One month ago, Trump was using anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed during his race against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.

But on Tuesday, the US president appeared to have changed his tune. During a 45-minute interview in the Oval Office, he told the New York Post, “He’s a smart guy,” as he answered questions about El-Sayed’s offer to rename “Medicare for All” as “Trumpcare”.

“He did a good job. He actually did a very good job,” the president said.

“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” he added. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” He did not give a date for the meeting.

Since the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, in which they lost their majorities in the US Senate and the House of Representatives, Trump has already indicated that he plans to make liberal use of his presidential veto to block “insane” Democratic policies.

However, he has also suggested that he may be open to negotiations, telling Fox News that he would “veto, veto, veto” but the Democrats would eventually call him hoping to do a deal.

“Congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job,” Trump said. “I congratulate them and look forward to working with them for the good of our country.”

In the New York Post interview, Trump praised El-Sayed’s idea of putting his name on the healthcare programme as “very smart”. He also said he and Democrats could work together on healthcare but “Obamacare hasn’t worked”.

Obamacare was an overhaul of the individual health insurance market under former President Barack Obama that had slowed increases in insurance costs and halved the number of uninsured Americans.

Trump added: “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point, I think they’re going to want to negotiate.”

El-Sayed first floated the idea of renaming the proposed healthcare plan on November 6 in an interview with Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan. “If he wants to pass Trumpcare for all, I’m OK with it. He seems to like to put his name on things,” El-Sayed said.

On November 12, he posted a mock-up of a gold “TrumpCare” insurance card bearing the president’s signature on X. “Donald, this is on the table,” he wrote. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

In a video posted on November 17, El-Sayed addressed the president as “habibi”, an Arabic term of affection. “Trumpcare for all. It’s really popular. People really want healthcare,” he said. “You can put your name all over it.”

The White House was initially dismissive. Spokesperson Allison Schuster called the proposal “Medicare for none” and described it as a socialist government takeover of healthcare.

But on Saturday, Trump reshared El-Sayed’s post on his Truth Social platform without comment. NBC News later reported that Vice President JD Vance’s office had contacted El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting.

On the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme the next day, El-Sayed called the plan “the ultimate Trump card”. He said he did not care what it was called as long as universal healthcare coverage passed. In a post on Monday, he wrote: “The point of winning elections is to do something good with the seat.”

The warmth displayed by the president is a reversal of his previous approach to El-Sayed.

During the election campaign, Trump repeatedly questioned El-Sayed’s loyalty to the US and tried to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood.

At an October 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump said he was there “to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator”. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the group, and he has denied any. Democrats denounced the attacks as targeting El-Sayed’s faith and his Egyptian heritage.

Vance told a rally in August that there was “something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil”.

El-Sayed, a physician and former head of Detroit’s Health Department, hit back throughout the campaign and at one point called Trump an “unserious fool”. He defeated Rogers to become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.

While most other wealthy countries have built universal health systems paid for from taxes, the US has relied largely on voluntary private insurance, leaving a substantial share of the population without coverage.

Despite decades of calls for national public insurance, it was not until 1965 that Washington created its two main public programmes: Medicare for people aged 65 and older, and Medicaid for people on low incomes.

Medicare, which also covers some younger people with disabilities, now serves nearly 70 million people.

Most Americans under 65 with health insurance rely on a patchwork of employer-provided insurance; private plans bought through the Obamacare, or Affordable Care Act, marketplaces; and Medicaid.

According to the US Census Bureau, 26.7 million people, or 7.9 percent of the population, were uninsured for all of 2025.

The Affordable Care Act, passed in 2010, made almost all lawfully present residents eligible for more affordable coverage than they had before. But taking it up remains largely voluntary, and millions still go without insurance, often citing cost as the barrier.

The US insurance model has proved expensive for the nation as a whole. The US spends more on healthcare than any other country in the world, and the gaps in coverage have deepened over five decades. In 1970, it spent about 7 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on healthcare, roughly in line with comparably wealthy countries, which averaged about 5 percent. By 2024, the latest government data available, that figure had risen to 18 percent of GDP.

Per person, the US spent an average of $14,775 on healthcare in 2024, compared to an average of $7,860 in comparably wealthy countries, according to Peterson-KFF.

Medicare for All is a policy proposal that would extend government insurance to every resident, not just those over 65, with disabilities or with low incomes.

The main bill on the table is Senator Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All Act. It would replace most private insurance with a single public plan with no premiums, deductibles or copayments.

Sanders has called on Democrats to start by reducing the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55.

Polling has traditionally been mixed but may now be rising. Pre-election polling by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organisation, suggested support for Medicare for All was 66 percent. Mollyann Brodie, who leads KFF’s polling, called it “the highest level of support … we’ve ever found”.

El-Sayed wants one public plan to cover every American “from cradle to grave”. In a book he cowrote, he described this as “an enhanced version of the traditional Medicare program that tens of millions of seniors rely on today”.

Doctor visits, prescription drugs and emergency care would be covered, and patients could see any participating provider without out-of-network charges.

Coverage would also no longer depend on a job or family circumstances. “Turn 26, get a job, lose a job, get married, get divorced: None of these would cost you your health insurance under Medicare for All,” he said in testimony to the Senate in 2022.

It comes down to the presidential veto.

In the November 3 midterms, Democrats flipped nine Republican-held Senate seats and won a 56-44 majority, including two independents who caucus with them. They also won a majority in the House – raising the number of their seats from 214 to 258. When the new Congress meets in January, it will be able to pass legislation without having to find Republican votes in the House and, on some measures, in the Senate.

But Trump may veto any bill. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers: 67 senators and, with all seats filled, 290 House members. Democrats are 11 votes short in the Senate alone, so an override would need a significant number of Republicans to break with the president, which is unlikely to happen.

Trump has signalled he will use the veto freely. A day before the midterms, he pledged to become “Mr Veto” if Democrats took control of Congress.

The easier route then is for Trump not to veto legislation. That is the bet El-Sayed is making: that Trump, ever the politician, might sign a popular bill if he gets the credit for it.

Analysts doubt the talks will deliver the system El-Sayed wants, but they see room for a deal of some kind.

“I do not think it will lead to anything like the single payer system El-Sayed favours,” Ian Lesser, a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, told Al Jazeera. “But as with Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani in New York, they may have a strangely positive relationship.”

In November last year, Trump heaped praise on then-mayor-elect Mamdani after the two held surprisingly cordial talks in the White House. That too was an about-turn from Trump, who, during the mayoral election campaign, had caricatured Mamdani as an anti-Semitic communist and threatened to strip him of his US citizenship while Mamdani called Trump a “despot” in his election victory speech.

Lesser said the El-Sayed exchange followed “very much the same pattern we saw with Mayor Mamdani: curiosity and the president’s focus on personalities above all”.

“The president could be inclined toward some new health reforms if he can put his own stamp on them,” Lesser added.

Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, said a meeting with El-Sayed would be part of an effort by Trump to salvage his legacy after the midterms defeat.
